# Scenario

@Polis-1998-490 were interested in modelling the presence/absence of lizards (<i>Uta sp.</i>) against the perimeter to area ratio of 19 islands in the Gulf of California.

![Uta lizard](../resources/uta.jpg){#fig-polis width="200" height="137"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}

ISLAND       RATIO   PA
------------ ------- ----
Bota         15.41   1
Cabeza       5.63    1
Cerraja      25.92   1
Coronadito   15.17   0
..           ..      ..

: Format of polis.csv data file {#tbl-polis .table-condensed}

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

------------ -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
**ISLAND**   Categorical listing of the name of the 19 islands used - variable not used in analysis.
**RATIO**    Ratio of perimeter to area of the island.
**PA**       Presence (1) or absence (0) of *Uta* lizards on island.
------------ -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

: Description of the variables in the polis data file {#tbl-polis1 .table-condensed}

:::
::::


The aim of the analysis is to investigate the relationship between island perimeter to area ratio and the presence/absence of Uta lizards.

# Read in the data

```{r}
#| label: readData
#| output: true
#| eval: true
polis <- read_csv("../data/polis.csv", trim_ws = TRUE)
```
# Bernoulli distribution

Bernoulli is a special case of binomial.

- Variance should equal 0
- Don't assume linearity


# Exploratory data analysis

```{r}
#| label: scatterplot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = PA, x = RATIO)) +
  geom_point()
#higher presence of lizards when island ration is small

#now add in curve to show the Bernoulli shape
polis |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = PA, x = RATIO)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method='glm', formula=y~x,
              method.args=list(family='binomial'))
```


The individual responses ($y_i$, observed presence/absence of Uta
lizards) are each expected to have been **independently** drawn from
Bernoulli (or binomial) distributions ($\mathcal{Bin}$). These
distributions represent all the possible presence/absences we could
have obtained at the specific ($i^th$) level of island perimeter to
area ratio.  Hence the $i^th$ presence/absence observation is expected
to have been drawn from a binomial distribution with a probability of
$\mu_i$ and size of ($n=1$).

The expected probabilities are related to the linear predictor
(intercept plus slope associated with perimeter to area ratio) via a
**logit** link.

We need to supply priors for each of the parameters to be estimated
($\beta_0$ and $\beta_1$).  Whilst we want these priors to be
sufficiently vague as to not influence the outcomes of the analysis
(and thus be equivalent to the frequentist analysis), we do not want
the priors to be so vague (wide) that they permit the MCMC sampler to
drift off into parameter space that is both illogical as well as
numerically awkward.

As a starting point, lets assign the following priors:

- $\beta_0$: Normal prior centred at 0 with a variance of 2.5
- $\beta_1$: Normal prior centred at 0 with a variance of 1

Note, when fitting models through either `rstanarm` or `brms`, the
priors assume that the predictor(s) have been centred and are to be
applied on the link scale.  In this case the link scale is an
identity.


Model formula:
$$
\begin{align}
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{Bin}(n, \pi_i)\\
OR \\
y_i &\sim{} \mathcal{Bernoulli}(\pi_i)\\
ln\left(\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}\right) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i\\
\beta_0 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\\
\beta_1 &\sim{} \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\\
\end{align}
$$


# Fit the model

```{r}
#| label: define formula
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#trials(1) represents the total number of trails, like 2 cats were female out of 7 total cats then it would be female|totalcats
polis_form <- bf(PA ~ RATIO, family = bernoulli(link = "logit"))

get_prior(polis_form, data = polis)

#median response should be ~0.5 because we have 0s and 1s.

qlogis(0.5) #how to back transform a logit (opposite of plogis)
#on logit scale the median will be 0

#priors have to be on the scale of the logit link
plogis(1)
plogis(-1)

#slope mean will always be 0
#slope variance will be 1

#intercept mean will be 0
#intercept variance will be 1

#set priors
priors <- prior(normal(0,1), class = 'Intercept') +
  prior(normal(0,1), class = 'b')
```

```{r}
#| label: prior only model
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

#stan uses no u turn sampler (NUTS)
polis_brm2 <- brm(polis_form,
                 data=polis,
                 prior=priors,
                 sample_prior="only",
                 iter=5000,
                 chains=3, cores=3, #one core per chain
                 warmup=1000,
                 thin=5,
                 backend="cmdstanr",
                 refresh=0)

```
```{r}
#| label: plot model polis_brm2
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm2 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#no matter what priors you use, the grey ribbon will go 0-1. We do have a gap at 20 so that's a good sign
#this plot isn't very informative for bernoulli
```
```{r}
#| label: sample from prior and data
#| eval: true
#| echo: true
#| cache: true

polis_brm3 <- update(polis_brm2, sample_prior = 'yes', refresh = 0)

```
```{r}
#| label: plot model polis_brm3
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> 
  conditional_effects() |> 
  plot(points = TRUE)

#now model looks much more refined
#and looks like data is driving the trend, not priors which is what we want
```
```{r}
#| label: examine all priors and posteriors
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> SUYR_prior_and_posterior()

#proof that priors are influential (thats what we want)
#this function helps show you what prior is problematic

#there's no way b posterior is the same as the prior, so no way priors are driving the trends
```

# MCMC sampling diagnostics

```{r}
#| label: traceplots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3$fit |> stan_trace()

polis_brm3$fit |> stan_trace(inc_warmup = TRUE)

#b_Intercept and Intercept are not the same because we forgot to center the x-axis/continuous variable
```

```{r}
#| label: autocorrelation plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3$fit |> stan_ac()
#standard to have a bar at 0
#at a lag of 1 (x-axis) we don't want to have large autocorrelation --> no bias between draws
#therefore, thinning was adequate
```

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#how well did chains converge
polis_brm3$fit |> stan_rhat()
#want values <1.01
#if they are above 1.01 then the chains were different from each other
      # ^ might need to add more iterations or check priors 
```

```{r}
#| label: effective sample size
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3$fit |> stan_ess()

#uses no u turn sampler (NUTS) --> not your actual data
#tells us how many draws were effective out of all of them
#want this to be >0.5, and closer to 1 the better
#its okay if they are <0.5, but this means the model isn't efficient and the priors were probably too large,
#causing the sampler to go too far
```

# Model validation
```{r}
#| label: posterior probs density overlay
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> pp_check(type = 'dens_overlay', ndraws=100)

#dark line is actual distribution of our data
#our model reconstructs the data quite well
```

```{r}
#| label: simulate residuals
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#fert.resids <- make_brms_dharma_res(fert_brm3, integerResponse = FALSE)
#testUniformity(fert.resids)
#plotResiduals(fert.resids)

#another option
preds <- polis_brm3 |> posterior_predict(ndraws=250, summary=FALSE)
polis.resids <- createDHARMa(simulatedResponse = t(preds),
                            observedResponse = polis$PA,
                            fittedPredictedResponse = apply(preds, 2, median),
                            integerResponse = TRUE)
polis.resids |> plot()

#QQ Plot: plots quantiles (median, upper, lower, etc)
#straight line applies that residuals follow nominated distribution (normal in this case)
#you want straight line
#KS: Smirnoff test for conformity to distribution --> if it was significant, maybe pay attention to it and see if you can change anything --> but don't blindly accept this
#Dispersion: ratio of variance to the mean --> for normal distribution we want close to 1
#Outlier test: if in red, check and see if it really is a problem

#residual plot: dont want any patterns (fan shape = unequal variances)
#we have 2 lines but that isn't a pattern, they were just binned
```

# Partial effects plots

```{r}
#| label: partial effects plots
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> conditional_effects() |> plot(points = TRUE)
```
# Model investigation
```{r}
#| label: summary
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> summary()

#summary values are always on the scale of the link function
#back transform intercept
plogis(4.43) #so when an island is really round (Ratio = 0), the probability of presence is 0.99
exp(4.41) #odds ratio: the lizards are 82 times more likely to be present when the island is round (Ratio = 0)

#now back transform slope
#can only be converted to odds, because the rate of change is never the same
exp(-0.26) #odds ratio: for every 1 unit change in Ratio, the odds of the lizard being present decline by a factor of 0.77
#OR a -23% decrease
100 * (0.77 -1)

#PROBABILITY SCALE:
# >0.85 = evidence for that is weak
# <0.85 = no evidence at all
# >0.9 = there is evidence
# >0.95 = the evidence is strong
```

```{r}
#| label: table on log odds scale
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

polis_brm3 |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*")) |> 
  exp() |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi,
                  rhat, 
                  ess_bulk,
                  P = ~mean(.x < 1))

#summary gives mean BUT this gives us the MEDIAN which is more robust

#our table is expentiated and exp(0) = 1 so that's why we use 1 in the calculation of P

#strong evidence of a negative relationship between lizard presence and perimeter to area ratio.

polis_brm3 |> bayes_R2(summary=FALSE) |> 
  median_hdci()
#y = R^2, 52% of variation in Presence/absence can be explained by perimter/area ratio
```

```{r}
#| label: LD50
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#at what point does the x-axis correspond to 0.5 PA? --> think of it as LD50

# - intercept / slope (on logit scale)

# should be around 20 RATIO

ed50 <- polis_brm3 |> 
  as_draws_df() |> 
  dplyr::select(matches("^b_.*")) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(ED50 = (-1*b_Intercept)/b_RATIO) |> 
  summarise_draws(median, 
                  HDInterval::hdi)

#ED50 is around 17.2 and we are 95% sure it's between 11.7 and 23.0
#no longer on logit link, it's on the scale of the predictors
```

# Further analyses

# Summary figure

```{r}
#| label: spaghetti plot
#| eval: true
#| echo: true

#use 100 values to predict a curve
newdata <- with(polis, data.frame(RATIO = seq(min(RATIO), max(RATIO), len = 100)))

head(newdata)

polis_pred <- polis_brm3 |> 
  emmeans(~RATIO, at = newdata) |> 
  gather_emmeans_draws() |> 
  dplyr::mutate(prob = plogis(.value)) #need to undo logit scale

ed50

#plot
p1 <- polis_pred |> 
  ggplot(aes(y = prob, x = RATIO)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = .draw), alpha = 0.02) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ed50$median[ed50$variable == "ED50"], color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ed50$lower[ed50$variable == "ED50"], linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = ed50$upper[ed50$variable == "ED50"], linetype = "dashed", color = "red", alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_x_continuous("Island perimeter:area") +
  scale_y_continuous("Probability of lizard presence") +
  theme_classic()
p1

ggsave(filename = "figure_2.pdf", p1, width = 6, height = 4, units = "in")
```
